An estimation of the $B^0_s\rightarrow K^+K^-$ decay time for $B^0_s$ mesons has been made with the help of around 37 picobarns of LHCb data from 2010. This measure allows for constraints on theories beyond the Standard Model that may influence the $B^0_s$ system and was found to be 1.440 picoseconds by employing two methods with varying degrees of uncertainty, specifically 0.096 (statistical) ± 0.008 (systematic) ± 0.003 (model-based).

This research paper focuses on the numerical solution of a stochastic control problem governed by a parabolic equation with the control variable affecting the diffusion coefficient, particularly with the presence of rough inputs; it establishes the convergence of a specific numerical discretization method and provides an alternative solution using a stochastic simulation technique known as the Monte-Carlo method.

Our in-depth examination of extremely energetic cosmic rays detected at the Pierre Auger Observatory reveals significant patterns of large-scale anisotropy. At the higher end of our energy range, a specific anisotropy signal was initially reported - namely, a right ascension-based dipolar modulation. To further investigate, we divided the most energetic group into three segments, and discovered that this anisotropy becomes increasingly pronounced with rising energy levels above 4 EeV, exhibiting an energy-dependent pattern that adheres to a power law with an index of 0.79 ± 0.19. We also discovered that the orientation of these anisotropy patterns supports their extragalactic origins, across all energy levels examined. Furthermore, an investigation of quadrupolar components revealed that they lacked sufficient statistical significance. We interpret our findings within the context of theoretical models proposing the distribution of extremely energetic cosmic sources and cosmic magnetic field dynamics.

The ATLAS detector at the LHC gathered p+Pb data with a centre of mass energy of 5.02 TeV and 25 nanobarns of integrated luminosity, enabling a comparison with interpolated pp measurements at 2.76 and 7 TeV. Owing to its sophisticated design and reliability, the ATLAS detector successfully collected a comprehensive dataset during heavy ion and proton-proton runs. As a result, it facilitated precise measurements of the nuclear modification factor, obtained by dividing charged particle yields from heavy ion collisions by their proton-proton counterparts in various centrality ranges and rapidity intervals. Furthermore, this analysis reveals a notable variation in the nuclear modification factor with transverse momentum, showing a more pronounced trend in more peripheral collisions.

Quantum mechanics can be explored on noncommutative spaces, characterized by specific commutation relations that define the structure constants of a Lie algebra. By transforming the coordinates into linear differential operators in a commuting momentum space, we can reformulate this issue into an ordinary quantum problem. These operators, representing the coordinates $\hat x_a$, have a form $-i\hat D_a = -iE_{ab}(p)\partial /\partial p_b$, where $E_{ab}$ can be expressed as an infinite series over the deformation parameter $\theta$. The deformed Hamiltonian $\hat H$ describes the motion on corresponding group manifolds with sizes proportional to $\theta^{-1}$, whose metrics also appear in certain infinite series of $\theta$. The matrices $E_{ab}$ can be represented in simple forms for certain algebras like $su(2)$ and $u(N)$. Additionally, our study has yielded new nonstandard metric formulas for all the spheres $S^n$, projective spaces $RP^n$, and $U(2)$.

In evaluating the potential of federated learning, we tested its performance in training deep learning models to analyze digitized tissue samples, specifically in a classification application involving the detection of tumor cells within whole-slide images. By simulating a FL environment with a large, diverse dataset of cancer images, we compared the results of training models through the FL process against traditional centralized learning. Our findings suggest that federated learning can produce models with accurate performance接近那 of centralized learning, while providing a secure and private approach to developing robust image analysis models, thus enabling more effective use of AI in tissue sample analysis.

In this study, a high-speed optical transmission system is demonstrated, achieving a data rate of 70 Gb/s using the on-off keying technique, over a distance of 18.8 km in a South China Sea submarine cable that lacks dispersion compensation.  Chromatic dispersion in this underwater cable causes four signal nulls in a 35 GHz bandwidth, severely hindering BER performance. To address this issue, a virtual-DAC dispersion compensation method via sound-to-data synthesis using an SPEAR sound card provides a low-cost, real-time solution for monitoring changing dispersion values and compensating accordingly, with a total data processing cost of under $100.  Our results indicate that shifting the receiver center frequency in real-time effectively mitigates the impact of dispersion, reducing the BER from 0.39 to 8.$^{−1}$ when comparing uncompensated to compensated scenarios.  This low-cost speech data synthesis approach provides an economical means of monitoring and compensating for changing dispersion values in underwater cables.  Although our prototype speaks to a PC for demonstration, the data processing can also be done with a microprocessor to remove the need for additional frequency shift devices, making it possible to implement adaptive D compensation with only a frequency agile receiver.

Deep Learning models like Temporal Convolutional Networks (TCNs) hold great promise for handling time-series data. TCNs leverage a technique called time-dilated convolution that poses an optimization challenge which typically demands significant experimentation. We've developed a technique to automate the dilation optimization process by casting it as a weight-pruning operation along the time axis. Our method learns dilation factors concurrently with weights during training and achieves notable gains in model compactness and inference efficiency without compromising accuracy. It produces a range of highly optimal TCN variants from a single starting model, surpassing the performance of custom-designed networks in both efficiency and accuracy.
This paper proves that any finite-dimensional Zinbiel algebra over a given field possesses a specific characteristic - nilpotency, building on a previous discovery that these algebras are solvable.

This study provides first-time data on the fluctuations of a specific angle, known as $\Psi_n$, and magnitude, known as $v_n$, related to particle flow, which have been determined using a newly developed technique for four-particle correlations. Researchers used ALICE to collect these data in high-energy Pb-Pb collisions at the LHC. Fluctuations in angle and magnitude were found to vary depending on transverse momentum and radial distance of particles from the center of the collision, also influenced by the collision speed. Notably, fluctuations in angle become less pronounced for transverse momentum above 10 GeV/c, while fluctuations in magnitude follow a similar pattern to the central charges, with a slight increase for higher transverse momentum in collisions at mid-speed.

The unified correspondence theory leverages the algebraic and order theoretic underpinnings of Sahlqvist correspondence to offer versatile tools for correspondence and canonicity across diverse semantic frameworks and signatures. These tools, specifically tailored to logics whose semantics rely on normal lattice expansions (DLEs), enable computation of first-order correspondents for inductive formulas using the algorithm ALBA. Conversely, our proposed method effectively employs ALBA's rules and algebraic language to reverse its computations in the DLE setting, thereby allowing the derivation of an inductive formula from its first-order correspondent.

This research focuses on addressing inconsistencies in data tables that contain missing values and functional relationships. Unlike conventional approaches that require adherence to these dependencies, our work aims to explore theories for handling instances that breach certain constraints. We have established a framework by extending the concept of data instances to include cases with inconsistencies. Within this framework, we have devised criteria for assessing data quality, such as completeness and uniqueness, and developed logical theories to evaluate these qualities. Notably, our approach offers a significant departure from traditional methods, as it enables assessment of data quality even in the presence of inconsistencies. To facilitate computation, we have generated algorithms with deterministic outcomes, but also explored options for non-deterministic solutions, as these yield more expressive logical specifications. Furthermore, we have examined the interplay between our proposed definitions and a fundamental principle, as well as the difficulty of determining logical implications under our framework, and provided an algorithm for querying data with inconsistencies.

This study presents a novel dynamic econometric model called Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates, specifically designed to analyze and forecast count-based time series data. Our research indicates that a score-driven approach is particularly effective in capturing the evolution of time-varying parameters and allows for modeling complex dynamics and shifts within such data sets. Furthermore, we have analyzed in-depth the theoretical characteristics of this model and conducted a thorough empirical analysis to demonstrate its effectiveness. Our findings show that Time-Varying Poisson AutoRegressive with external covariates achieves superior forecasting performance in comparison to both established count data models and generalized linear regression methods, particularly for short-term predictions.

We introduce Neural Descriptor Fields (NDFs), a novel object representation that
replicates both object points and relative poses in relation to a target, using
category-level descriptors. We apply this representation in object manipulation,
with the aim of repeating tasks on new object instances from the same category
after watching a single demonstration. To achieve this, we use optimization to
find the descriptor parameters from both visual data and geometric constraints.
We focus on manipulating circular objects based solely on visual and spatial
information, without using touch feedback. Our experiments show that with just
one demonstration, we can successfully transfer tasks across both 2D rotations
and 3D transformations of a variety of everyday object types. In collaboration
with researchers from MIT, our work has been further refined and is now presented
at the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation (ICRA).

The SiD Detector is one of the two validated detector designs for the future ILC, specifically tailored to meet precision demands for the Higgs boson and other research areas while maintaining an adaptable sensitivity to diverse potential discoveries. The SiD's robust silicon vertex and tracking system, complemented by its central high-resolution calorimeter suite, enables precise momentum determination and accurate energy measurement. The outer iron-return-yoke and highly sensitive muon system ensure accurate muon detection and momentum determination within the SiD's design. This presentation outlines the SiD's track system design, featuring a finely spaced 4-layer structure with high hit resolution and minimal impact on particle flow. Furthermore, the SiD's concept of using a solid muon system, featuring a block structure with excellent tracking capabilities and reasonable cost, is described. Using solid-state silicon muon tracks as a baseline for particle identification, the muon system ensures accurate muon tagging, complementing the calorimeters in their respective strengths of measuring momentum for different particles.

We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven red giant members in the globular cluster Tononzintla 2. We used the APOGEE-2 near-infrared spectra to examine the abundance levels of multiple chemical species in these stars. The findings showed a moderate metal content and the absence of an internal variation in metal abundance. Tononzintla 2 displayed an increased presence of alpha-enrichment which aligns with patterns observed in other rich-metallic galactic clusters. A nitrogen spread was discovered in Tononzintla 2 with multiple nitrogen-rich stars residing within it, significantly above average levels for this region, suggesting a multi-generational population within the cluster that consists of first-generation nitrogen-abundance members. A [Ce/Fe] spread was identified and found to correlate with nitrogen, suggesting a relatively minor, s-process enriched population within the cluster which was above average for this region. A comparison was made between multiple chemical patterns within Galaxy clusters and multiple abundance levels, which showed that Galaxy clusters' patterns fit best with an intermediate category between two less-mixed clusters.

The Isabelle Archive of Formal Proofs has amassed substantial size over recent years, representing an impressive compilation of research and offering a diverse range of opportunities for statistical exploration in the field of theorem proving. Despite the numerous contributions produced so far, the ever-expanding nature of the archive still poses certain challenges: locating specific content has become increasingly difficult, making it essential to prioritize reuse and clarity of comprehension. This thesis proposal outlines my research objectives, which focus on these concerns, as well as initial findings, which reveal that the Isabelle Archive exhibits characteristics suitable for such analysis, as evidenced by ways in which the difficulty of accessing content scales with the archive's size, alongside observations on the distribution of dependencies among the theories within the archive.

Using the functional renormalization group at the next-to-leading order in the derivative expansion, we have updated the position of the Yang-Lee edge singularity for O(N) universality classes in classic scenarios. Specifically for QCD's relevant universality classes in three dimensions, we have determined $|z_c|/R_\chi^{1/\gamma}$ to be approximately 1.607, 1.589 for $N=2, 4$ respectively. Alternatively, we have previously found $|z_c|$ to be around 2.03, 1.68 for $N=2, 4$ although these earlier results have a larger systematic uncertainty.

In statistics and machine learning, it is frequently essential to establish whether a basic optimization method on a non-convex function can eventually enter a region where the function becomes locally convex. To address this, we developed an inequality that enables us to analyze the properties of the optimization landscape surrounding the solutions produced by an approximate message passing (AMP) algorithm. Specifically, we applied our inequality to demonstrate the local convexity of a particular TAP free energy function, which is relevant to the Z2 synchronization problem and the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick model. Additionally, our inequality led to a local convexity result for a non-convex regularized least-squares function associated with a Z2 synchronization model, making it possible to prove a new 'information theory meets optimization' theorem. This theorem confirms that a localized fixed point of the AMP algorithm is surrounded by a locally convex optimization landscape, thereby ensuring that any initial starting point within this neighborhood will allow an iterative application of AMP to converge and reveal the message's spectrum.

Modern metasurfaces, at the intersection of advanced technology and science,  
constitute an intricate field, involving electromagnetic systems characterized by  
thin, expansive, and minutely featured particles that can also vary spatially,  
temporally, and linearly.  To tackle this intricacy, researchers need to employ a  
unified approach, integrating theoretical design and analysis methods, supported  
by an established framework.  Recent breakthroughs, facilitated by Generalized  
Sheet Transition Conditions in combination with surface susceptibilities,  
now enable designers to develop intricate metasurfaces, addressing longstanding  
challenges.  This paper delves into computational modeling of these complex  
structures through GSTC-susceptibility methodology and underscores its critical  
importance in the holistic design of metasurfaces, reviewing the evolution of  
recent frequency and time-domain computational methods.

The primary objective of this research is to validate the smooth local orbital linearization theorem for smooth vector fields with a full set of nearby first integrals, especially those at nondegenerate singular points. This theoretical validation relies heavily on key concepts, including the formal orbital linearization theorem, the orbital formal first bethe-entropy theorem, and the formal orbital normal form.

This report outlines a deep learning approach known as the Electron Correlation
Potential Neural Network (eCPNN), which can learn simplified potential functions
that accurately capture the intricate instantaneous relationships among electrons
within complex atomic systems. Trained in an unsupervised manner with constrained
data derived from Full Configuration Interaction one-electron density functions, the
eCPNN model effectively predicts total atomic energies with remarkable precision.

We have serendipitously identified a massive arc-like structure, dubbed a Giant Arc, which lies at a redshift of approximately 0.8. Spanning nearly 1 billion light-years, this feature exhibits remarkable symmetry when viewed from space. It was discovered through a novel approach using intervening magnesium-absorbing systems in the light from background quasars. Our analysis leverages a range of techniques: hierarchical clustering, a statistical test, and power spectrum analysis - each method providing unique insights, which together suggest the presence of a massive structure at around 4.5 to 4.8 sigma confidence levels. We employed multiple statistical tests to mitigate any biases that could influence our findings, which suggest that the arc-like feature is an overdensity with a density ratio of about 1.3, with a 30% margin of error. The Giant Arc represents one of the largest and most intriguing examples of a massive cosmic structure that could challenge the cosmological principle underpinning our current understanding of the universe. It may be an early stage in the formation of a massive structure, such as the Sloan Great Wall, which would have emerged around halfway through the universe's age.

While using photometry from stars to monitor the atmosphere may seem uncomplicated for optical astrophysics, achieving a precision of 0.01 for measuring the aerosol depth has been challenging. By taking wide-field photometry over a broad altitude range, the aerosol depth can be determined quickly, regardless of the system's absolute calibration, and even provides calibration as a by-product. Our team used extensive data from the FRAM telescope at the Pierre Auger Observatory and a similar telescope at the Cherenkov Telescope Array site to improve the precision of this technique to a precision of possibly 0.01. To accomplish this, we conducted precise laboratory measurements of the system's response to varying light intensities and spectra to counter the limitations of non-linear CCD detectors under observation conditions.

Recently, estimating a 6D object pose using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) has gained significant interest. Literature can be broadly categorized into two main areas based on whether intermediate cues are employed: direct methods and two-stage pipelines. In the latter category, CNN regresses intermediate cues such as object coordinates or virtual control points instead of pose parameters in the initial stage. Object pose is then resolved through the construction of correspondence constraints utilizing these intermediate cues. This study concentrates on refining two-stage pipelines by combining two distinct concepts: projection constraints and correspondence constraints. Rather than relying on conventional approaches to generate projections and correspondences, we adopt an innovative strategy based on projection constraints. By employing the concept of virtual control points, we derive a set of 2D projections corresponding to predefined 6D pose control points in 3D Euclidean space. These virtual control points projections are then incorporated into a closure constraint formulation called the Least Absolute Sparse Error (LASE) to estimate object pose in the presence of occlusions and outliers. Experiments conducted on standard object pose estimation benchmarks demonstrate the superior performance of LASE in comparison to traditional two-stage pipelines.

Peridynamic theories have seen a significant expansion in their application across multiple disciplines, due to their ability to model and track discontinuity formation within materials. Bond-based Peridynamics, despite its modeling restrictions, has become a widely-used approach in numerical simulations because of its ease of implementation and ability to incorporate the free energy concept for use as a driving force in simulations. However, a major limitation arises from Bond-based Peridynamics' inability to accurately represent all interatomic forces within a given potential, resulting in an inconsistent force closure. This inconsistency hinders the accurate modeling of highly dynamic phenomena, characterized by discontinuities such as material separation. This study proposes two methods to address this shortcoming, by introducing new inter-point relationships that reflect specific features of the material's equilibrium structure, thus improving the consistency of the force closure and enabling more precise simulation of discontinuity formation. Method one results in a model with enhanced performance at the cost of reduced order accuracy, whereas Method two maintains the model's accuracy but with reduced performance. This difference in outcome underscores the trade-off between introducing new length-scale parameters into existing material models and increasing new material models for a specific process.

We present GGLasso, a Python library designed to address General Graphical Lasso
challenges. Based on the original work of Friedman (2007), Graphical Lasso
estimates a sparsely constructed inverse covariance matrix $\Theta$ from
multivariate Gaussian data $\mathcal{X}$, initially introduced by Dempster (1972)
under Covariance Selection. The framework has been expanded to accommodate
hidden variables in Chandrasekaran (2012) and can jointly estimate multiple
inverse covariance matrices, as shown in Danaher (2014) and Tomasi (2019). The
GGLasso package supports the resolution of diverse formulations and notable
subcases like Graphical Lasso with latent variables, Group, and Fused Graphical Lasso.

Numerous numerical techniques for resolving stochastic differential equations in molecular dynamics simulations focus on obtaining precise configurational averages. These methods accurately reproduce the Boltzmann distribution and correlation functions within biomolecules, particularly stochastic boundary methods and related algorithms such as the normal hierarchy method. These algorithms redivide the biomolecule's degrees of freedom into equalized folders according to their influence on the biomolecule's energy, thereby minimizing fluctuations and enhancing efficiency. By incorporating the concept of folder width with the folder's boundary surface area, a new method is introduced that optimizes the StCM framework, yielding results comparable to the normal hierarchy method but two to three times faster, thereby reducing computation time for configurational averages by a factor of N, where N is the number of degrees of freedom biomolecules possess.

Numerical relativity simulations allow us to study how binary black hole mergers interact with their surroundings. However, these simulations typically focus on merging spins aligned with the binary axis. In a separate investigation, we examine the responses of matter to unequal mass and multi-oriented binary black holes. Using simulations, we analyze the effectiveness of gravitational wave templates that account for dark matter around the binary, particularly in comparison to models without the surrounding matter. Our findings suggest that the gravitational waves produced by a dark matter binary have an average amplitude that's 10% lower than those from a binary with no surrounding matter, with the difference increasing to 30% for binaries containing less massive dark matter. These findings indicate that binary dark matter could potentially be distinguished from its counter part without surrounding matter, assuming sufficient sensitivity in future detectors. Additionally, we discover that in dark matter binaries, the inner stability orbit is about 15 times the mass of the smaller black hole, while the inner stable orbit in matter binaries without surrounding dark matter is significantly closer, at 4.2 times the mass of the smaller black hole, or about 9% of the total mass of the binary.

We tackle the persistent issue of exponential stability for a stretched Euler-Bernoulli beam on a star-shaped graph with three equal branches. The outer points where these branches meet are fixed while rotating. The inner point is capable of moving in two ways, with rotational movement influenced by both elasticity and friction. A detailed analysis in a Hilbert space reveals how the spectrum's asymptotic distribution and structure evolve. It demonstrates that specific eigenvector characteristics form a complete and orthonormal basis. Consequently, we derive the exponential stability of the associated semigroup directly. Notably, we show that under these connectivity conditions, stability is guaranteed even in the absence of elasticity along the edges.

Researchers utilized acoustic lenses composed of PMMA to increase the detection area of sensitive devices and improve resolution but discovered these lenses introduced image distortion. This problem was investigated and a new lens material called Stycast 1090SI was proposed as an alternative. The acoustic properties of this novel material were examined alongside PMMA to determine its feasibility. Computational simulations and practical tests using two different materials, PMMA and Stycast 1090SI, showed both materials significantly enhance the detection capabilities of sensitive devices. Notably, the Stycast lens exhibited lower levels of distortion compared to the PMMA lens, which could have implications for photoacoustic tomography technology.

Our new method calculates a variation of eigenvector centrality for multi-layered networks that incorporate node importance across different layers. In these networks, defined by separate interconnected graphs without connections between different layers, the value of a node's centrality is determined by the sum of the values of the connected nodes within each specific layer, similar to traditional eigenvector centrality calculations. Unlike standard approaches, our approach takes into account the relationships between different network layers and their respective impact on the centrality values. Unlike current multi-layer eigenvector centrality frameworks that account for inter-layer connections, our approach uses a separate set of equations that can be solved using a hybrid algorithm.

We tackle the issue of non-blind deblurring and demosaicking on noisy raw images using a learning-based approach tailored to handle these images directly, with an innovative new component that simultaneously demosaicks and deblurs them in an interpretable way. To train this model, we utilize real-world camera data transformed into raw images through a realistic process, mimicking real-world camera functions. By doing so, we demonstrate the advantages of our single-stage model over traditional approaches combining demosaicking and deblurring modules, according to objective performance metrics. Additionally, our method is capable of removing a camera's intrinsic blurring effect, which effectively enables deblurring of sharper images from actual pictures.

Recently, we generated the $R$-Poincar\'e algebra using deformed Poisson brackets, 
which effectively replicate the Fock coordinate transformation. This transformation 
corresponds to a de Sitter spacetime. In this study, we formulate the Dirac equation within 
$R$-Minkowski spacetime and establish that it is analogous to the Dirac equation defined 
within the de Sitter spacetime, described by its conformally flat metric. We then propose 
a novel strategy to solve the Dirac equation within the de Sitter spacetime by adopting 
the Schr\"{o}dinger picture.

This study introduces an open source Python framework that utilizes background knowledge and observational data for the purpose of inferring causal relationships. This framework is comprised of the 'cdt' package, which executes a comprehensive causal discovery process to identify the causal interactions and the causal network structure among the variables, drawing from established methodologies including those from 'Bnlearn' and 'Pcalg', in addition to pairwise algorithms like ANM. The framework is available on GitHub under the terms of the permissive MIT License.

This study investigates how spheres interact with water upon impact, specifically the process known as surface seal that occurs as the sphere enters the water's surface. This surface seal regime, found between low and high-speed impact velocities, features a distinctive "splash dome" formation. Empirical rules describing when the splash dome closes ("pinch-off time") generally hold for both slow-moving and fast-moving spheres, yet require further refinement, especially in the middle speed range. In fact, at mid-range speeds, pinch-off times relate differently to fluid dynamics than they do at either low or high speeds, indicating that increased pressures inside the formed cavity play a significant role. In addition, our findings include the shift from the deeper water-entrapment phenomenon to the surface-seal regime, and observations on the partial-seal, rippling-cavity-surface, and secondary pinch-off stages of water-entry interactions.

A well-known hypothesis posits that gravity at a quantum level must be devoid of universal symmetries. We studied an array of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories to uncover the range of universal symmetries potentially present and then investigated why they are avoided. Generalized $\theta$-terms emerge as crucial elements in these theories. These $\theta$-terms generate nonlinear connections between axion fields and quadratic gauge field strengths which can be used to break many universal symmetries. If we consider fixed values for the moduli, the effective four-dimensional theories develop Type IIB descendants that consist of three-form fields interacting with their duals through magnetic terms similar to the $\theta$-terms in four dimensions. These interactions result in one of the most comprehensive realizations of symmetry avoidance, where not only is a $U(1)$ symmetry lacking, as has been previously discussed in relation to the electron's charge, but so is a broader $U(1)$ symmetry encompassing the masses of states across all scalar towers - both semi-classical and transcendentally natured.

Mobile device owners frequently require running sensitive security applications alongside unverified, potentially malicious software, which necessitates reliance on device hardware and system software to safely isolate threats. 

This often misplaced trust is the foundation on which our objective is built – namely to minimize the reliance on device hardware and software components for users to withstand cyber threats. 

We introduce an innovative multi-domain hardware setup consisting of isolated sections, where programs are partitioned statically to prevent malicious interaction. 

A few key hardware components with proven security functionality are integrated to grant secure temporary access to processing resources and external input/output interfaces simultaneously.

To manage these hardware components, we introduce OctopOS, a unique OS comprising several secure subsystems working together in distrust. 

We showcase a functioning prototype, incorporating our hardware and software, utilizing a combined CPU-FPGA board with an acceptable additional hardware expense in comparison to existing SoCs. 

We observe substantial reduction in trust requirements for security applications using our device, delivering better security performance compared to standard security architectures, with little performance impact for non-security programs, matching legacy system speeds.

We investigated the challenges of robust reinforcement learning in scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates rewards and transition probabilities. The adversary's influence is confined to no more than an $\epsilon$ fraction of all training episodes. Notably, this attack model surpasses previously considered methods. We successfully developed an $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$-optimal strategy, which we believe to be near-universally effective thanks to the gradient-based nature of policy optimization. Our findings indicate that NP-hard approach may be unnecessary. In contrast to methods resilient to solely corrupted rewards, our results highlight that it is crucial to address transition probability corruption. Furthermore, we determined that addressing transition probability corruption necessitates an $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-optimal response, which merely reinforces the significance of our solution being primarily $\mathcal{O}(\epsilon)$-optimal. To facilitate this, we proposed NPG-A, a natural policy gradient algorithm with an adaptive learning rate, which achieves this $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\epsilon})$-plus performance component.

We uncover an unselectable version of the box game paradox, featuring players making remarkably accurate predictions of unknown real numbers without access to relevant information. Additionally, our analysis confirms the requirement of choice in solving the classic problem and examines alternative configurations of the game.

Our calculations using first-principles methods reveal that cubanite exhibits unusual orbital selectivity, with electrons occupying certain molecular orbitals while being localized in other atomic ones. This phenomenon is exceptionally rare in 3d transition metal compounds, providing a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed lack of charge disproportionation, anomalous Mössbauer spectra, and ferromagnetic coupling between adjacent iron ions.

A burgeoning field in quantum physics, known as multi-phonon physics, is driving research and development for both fundamental understanding and applications in metrology and communication systems. Quantum acoustic resonators serve as the ideal testing ground for multi-phonon phenomena through a combination of theoretical and experimental studies. The specific system studied consists of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity, and has exhibited remarkable multi-phonon properties, albeit previously described with a simplistic two-level quantum dot model. However, by incorporating a more advanced model that accounts for a greater complexity, specifically a dark exciton above a J=1 phonon by just one photon, researchers can uncover the existence of an "acoustic Rabi anhydride" state. This new model enables precise prediction of several four-phonon phenomena that were not previously observable with the earlier model. Moreover, it reveals that dark excitons, which have a tendency to decay slowly, are no longer hindrances by small addition of bright exciton character, further facilitated by the quantum dot-coustic system, and can be utilized as efficient sources of multiple phonons.

Our investigation focuses on a 2D electronic lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group.  We're examining a herringbone lattice with two types of glide symmetries in perpendicular directions using a nearest-neighbor tight-binding model. This model contains horizontal and vertical hopping terms and reveals two distinct non-equivalent Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These cones can be modified through various perturbations of the Hamiltonian. These perturbations disrupt the lattice symmetries by applying differing onsite potentials at the lattice sites, which causes the Dirac cones to collapse into semi-Dirac cones and nodal lines along the high-symmetry paths. Next, we applied a dimerization to the hopping terms and observed the migration of the Dirac cones across the first Brillouin zone along curved trajectories. Additionally, we outline the potential realization of this model using CO atoms on top of a Cu(111) surface.

Quantum states known as single-photon catalyzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated via quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. These states occur when a coherent state and a single-photon state interact in two input ports, and a photon is detected in a specific output channel. We examine the success probabilities associated with detecting these states, as they vary depending on the catalytic device used. Notably, our analysis reveals that states produced by beam splitters and parametric amplifiers exhibit the same characteristics when analyzing the distribution of photons. We thoroughly investigate the unique quantum properties of SPCCSs, including sub-Poisson statistics, anti-bunching effects, and quadrature squeezing. These findings demonstrate that SPCCSs possess abundant non-classical behavior, thereby conferring a quantum advantage for executing various technological tasks.

In General Relativity using the Newman-Penrose formalism, the use of bivectors plays a key role in identifying the precise solutions to Einstein's field equations. This review focuses on explaining the fundamental principles and detailed calculations of bivectors within the Newman-Penrose formalism, specifically by converting a complex self-dual electromagnetic field from the standard Minkowski space basis to the complex null tetrad basis. As a result, we derive the complex coefficients of the Weyl tensor in the context of Newman-Penrose formalism.

A recent framework combining artificial neural networks and mixed integer linear programming for designing chemical compounds has been built upon to create a new method for polymer inference. This new method incorporates a unique way of depicting polymers using monomers, new descriptors that capture their structure, and employs linear regression in the predictive framework. Computational trials have demonstrated that the proposed approach excels in predicting specific chemical properties in polymers, also successfully modeling compounds composed of up to 50 non-hydrogen atoms within a monomeric structure.

This paper presents a unified approach to addressing certain complex optimization challenges. Problems of control, estimation, and system design can be redefined as optimization problems subject to specific constraints. However, given the infinite dimensionality of these issues, it becomes necessary to employ numerical techniques to approximate a solution. We explore specific methods used in simultaneous direct approaches, specifically the transcription process. Our focus is on collocation, residual integration, and Runge-Kutta schemes, highlighting their applications to a case study related to the ventilator shortage during the COVID-19 pandemic. Our study investigated the possibility of ventilating more than one patient on a single ventilator by estimating patient parameters with a limited number of flow rate measurements, modifying air flow resistance, and controlling the ventilator's pressure to ensure desired tidal volumes for both patients.

Identifying tumors in the esophagus from CT scans can be very difficult for humans or computer systems due to low contrast, the varying shape of the esophagus, and the presence of external objects such as feeding tubes. To compensate for these difficulties, doctors often rely on specialized software that uses automatic segmentation technology to outline the tumors. However, creating these automated systems requires high-quality data annotated by experts, a process that is both time-consuming and expensive. As an initial step toward developing more efficient computer systems for tumor segmentation, this study explores various regularisation methods commonly used in semi-supervised and self-supervised segmentation. Building upon previous work, our study expands the range of evaluation parameters and incorporates two additional factors not previously examined: tumor segmentation and CT scans corrected for bone-artifacts. Our study aims to identify and promote simple regularisation techniques that can be used as a foundation for more sophisticated computer systems in tumor segmentation projects.

The expense associated with drilling offshore wells is significant and these sites frequently contain complex hydrocarbon reservoirs. Achieving optimal well placement and reducing costs necessitates real-time geosteering. This process is usually supported by up-to-date formation evaluations derived from the interpretation of well logs acquired during drilling. For this application, a reliable, fast, and robust approach to well-log interpretation in offshore environments has been absent. A profound issue in well-log interpretation lies in the vast array of available estimators, each suited to different formation types, combined with the unknown accuracy of data acquired during drilling. A Bayesian framework for well-log interpretation has been developed, incorporating multiple models and incorporating real-time formation assessments into a rigorous stochastic optimization scheme. This new algorithm was implemented and tested using data from the Aquitaine Margin, utilizing a surface seismic dataset to identify potential layer boundaries and a dataset from four production wells to validate the results. The algorithm successfully handled various types of well logs and provided estimates of impedance values that aligned with those obtained from adjacent wells and known production targets. Moreover, the uncertainty associated with these estimates could be accurately represented. Although restricted to one-dimensional reservoirs, the method's efficiency and capacity to integrate real-time data and account for well logs' inherent diversity make it an ideal solution for well-log interpretation in challenging marine environments.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a fundamental task in natural language processing and a core extraction technique, extensively used to retrieve text-based information for further analysis. One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which are suitable for non-overlapping or simply nested entities but ineffective for highly overlapping entities with a hierarchical structure. This study proposes a novel hierarchical model for nested named entities, modeling them as non-overlapping, nested, or overlapping entities based on their textual representation. Our experimental evaluation on three public datasets, SemEval-2014, Annotated Wikipedia Chinese Entities, and AG News, demonstrates that our hierarchical model achieves superior performance over current state-of-the-art models for nested NER.

We extend the use of tropical methods to counting in arithmetic problems, such as enumerating objects in higher-dimensional spaces using values from specific algebraic structures, over fields that have been modified to have special values, such as plane quartics with specific tangent properties as a reference. We look at curves defined by equations that are smooth, or at least have smooth properties in certain situations, over such modified fields. We express obstacles to counting these curves and their associated tangencies by altering the structure of these curves and their starting properties, focusing on edges and how they are affected. We show that by understanding how these curves and their starting properties change when modified, we can calculate the relative importance of these curves when counting them, and that this calculation can be made using a combination of these curves and their starting properties, and that this calculation is consistent when similar curves are compared. This consistent calculation relies on how these curves and their starting properties are organized in a specific way, such as being arranged in a circle.
